title: Most Used Words, Ties Alphabetical
statement:
You get a list words and a number k. Return the k words that occur most often, each word once.

Order the result from the most frequent word to the least frequent. Words with the same count are ordered alphabetically (ordinary string order), and that tie-break also decides which words make the cut at the boundary.

k is never larger than the number of distinct words.

examples.why: All three words appear twice. The tie-break keeps the two alphabetically first ones, so "pear" is left out.
"a" leads with 2. "b" and "c" tie at 1 and go alphabetically, not in the order they first appeared.

hints: Start by counting how often each word occurs. Then the question is only about ordering those (word, count) pairs.
Sorting the distinct words by count descending, then alphabetically, already works. Can you avoid sorting all of them when k is small?

Keep a heap of at most k words whose top is the current worst candidate: the lowest count, and for equal counts the alphabetically largest word. Push each word, pop when the heap grows past k, then read it out in reverse.

explain.intuition:
First count. After that, each distinct word has a score, and you want the best k under one ordering: higher count first, and for equal counts the alphabetically smaller word first. Sorting all distinct words by that ordering and taking the first k is correct and simple.

When there are many distinct words and k is small, a heap of size k saves work. The heap keeps the k best words seen so far, with the worst of them on top so it can be thrown out the moment something better arrives. "Worst" uses the same ordering turned around: lower count, or same count and alphabetically later. The tie-break must be flipped too, which is the step people get wrong.
steps: Count each word in a hash map.
Push each distinct word into a heap whose top is the worst word: smallest count, ties broken by the alphabetically largest word.
Whenever the heap holds more than k words, pop the top.
Pop everything that is left. It comes out worst first, so reverse it before returning.
pitfalls: Flipping the count for the heap but not the tie-break. Then among tied words the heap throws away the alphabetically first one, which is the one you must keep.
Breaking ties by first appearance, which is what an insertion-ordered Map gives you for free. With ["c", "b", "c", "b"] and k = 1 the answer is ["b"], although "c" came first.
Returning words more than once because the heap was fed every occurrence instead of every distinct word.

complexity.time: O(n + m log k), m distinct words

solutions.title: Count, then sort the distinct words
solutions.idea: Count with a hash map, sort distinct words by count descending and then alphabetically, take the first k.

solutions.title: Heap of the k best, worst on top
solutions.idea: Keep at most k candidates in a heap ordered so the weakest one is on top; evict it when a (k+1)-th word arrives.

followups: The words arrive as an endless stream and you must report the top k at any moment. What do you keep?
Could bucket sort by count beat O(m log k)? What does it cost for the alphabetical tie-break?
